claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy subsets are primarily controlled by variations in lattice distortion.
Differences in atomic size mismatch produce variations in lattice distortion.
Changes in dislocation mobility influence strength and ductility.
The investigated equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Selectively reducing or replacing elements can vary atomic size mismatch and the degree of lattice distortion while retaining the FCC phase.
Local lattice distortion can be represented by strain fields around solute atoms and compositional heterogeneity.
Greater lattice distortion caused by larger atomic size differences impedes dislocation movement.
Enhanced solute drag and local stress fields mediate the impediment of dislocation movement.
Impeded dislocation movement leads to higher yield strength.
Greater lattice distortion alters deformation pathways relative to alloys with lower distortion.
FCC subsets with greater atomic size mismatch than the equiatomic quinary baseline will have increased yield strength.
FCC subsets with greater atomic size mismatch than the equiatomic quinary baseline will exhibit modified ductility and shifted stress-strain responses.
Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni has an intermediate level of lattice distortion relative to the proposed alloy series.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys subjected to similar thermomechanical processing.
The proposed relationship may not apply to multiphase alloys or alloys dominated by electronic or magnetic interactions.
Electronic or magnetic effects may also contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
